title: Anthropic’s amended S-1 puts third-quarter revenue at $16.96 billion and the net loss at $23.29 billion. Turkey opened a competition probe of Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode, and ordered interim terms. The New York Times sued Brave over an index the complaint says holds more than 30 billion pages. Elon Musk said serving Grok Bot cost too much next to revenue, and did not say the new limit. OpenAI’s Georgia pilot includes up to 1,000 megawatts the campus can stop drawing, and the campus is not running.
summary: On Monday 2 November 2026 Anthropic filed an amendment to its S-1. Reuters said third-quarter revenue was $16.96 billion, up 47% from the quarter before, and that the net loss was $23.29 billion. Reuters said the operating loss was $567 million, after operating income of $974 million the quarter before. CNBC, the same day, said roughly $17 billion of third-quarter revenue, a nine-month revenue of $33.24 billion, and a nine-month net loss of $104 billion, most of it from the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Both said purchase and lease commitments were about $895.4 billion. On 2 November Turkey’s Competition Authority announced an investigation of Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode, and interim measures decided at its 8 October meeting. The announcement is not a finding that Google broke the law. On 2 November the New York Times sued Brave Software in Manhattan. TechCrunch said a separate suit, filed the same day by the New York Daily News, the Chicago Tribune and the Orlando Sentinel, makes a similar claim. The Times complaint, as TechCrunch quotes it, says Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages. On Sunday 1 November Elon Musk replied on X that the cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue. TechCrunch, on 2 November, said he has not said how subscribers’ limits change. On 2 November OpenAI announced the Grid Protectors Program and said a planned campus in Effingham County, Georgia, is still in development. The post says the Georgia Power agreement includes up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response.
uncertainty: Reuters says third-quarter revenue was $16.96 billion. CNBC, the same morning, says roughly $17 billion and about 1,127% above the same quarter a year earlier. Those are two roundings of one filing, not two revenues. CNBC’s nine-month net loss of $104 billion is not the operating loss. CNBC says most of it was the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Reuters’s operating loss of $567 million is the line for running the business in the quarter. Reuters does not print the prior quarter’s revenue in dollars, only that revenue had risen 144% in that quarter. Do not back into a dollar figure. The $895.4 billion is a commitment, as both outlets describe the filing. Reuters says about $69.8 billion of it is due in the 12 months after 30 September 2026, and that the company expects to incur nearly half before 31 December 2030. It is not a bill that has been paid, and it is not a quarterly expense. Turkey’s 2 November page announces an investigation and interim measures. The preliminary inquiry decision is dated 27 August 2026. The interim-measures decision is dated 8 October 2026. The page says the indications reached “strong suspicion.” It does not say a violation was found, and it does not name a fine. The “more than 30 billion” pages are what TechCrunch says the Times complaint says. The Verge’s quotes from the Times, from the other papers’ lawyer, and from Perplexity are statements, not findings. TechCrunch says Brave did not immediately comment. The Verge says Brave, Anthropic, Mistral, SpaceXSI and Cohere did not immediately reply. Perplexity did. TechCrunch’s “roughly $250 million” raised is what it attributes to private-market trackers, not to a Brave filing, so it is not used below. On Grok Bot, “as low as 50% to 100%” is TechCrunch’s report of what some users posted. It is not a meter reading from SpaceX. Musk’s sentence does not say the weekly allowance was cut by a stated amount, and TechCrunch says he has not said how limits change from here. The 52% of income, the $431 million profit and the $1.2 billion of Cursor costs are what TechCrunch says a filing last month already showed. They are not new figures from this weekend. OpenAI’s “roughly 700,000 households” is its own scale for up to 1,000 megawatts. It is not a count of homes that have received power. The campus is still in development. Georgia Power’s approximately $950 million a year from 2029, and at least $15 a month, are what OpenAI says the utility projects from a portfolio of large-load agreements and expected growth, including Project Camellia. They are not a saving OpenAI attributes to Effingham alone. The post’s line that U.S. data center capacity is projected to exceed 100 gigawatts by 2030 cites a link and does not name the study in the paragraph, so that figure is left out.

stories.theme: Anthropic’s amended S-1 shows $16.96 billion of third-quarter revenue and a $23.29 billion net loss
stories.changed: On Monday 2 November 2026 Anthropic filed an amendment to the S-1 it had filed the week before. The first filing had stopped at the first half of the year. Reuters said the amendment shows third-quarter revenue of $16.96 billion, up 47% from the quarter before. Reuters said revenue had risen 144% in the second quarter, and that the pace slowed. CNBC, the same day, said Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in the third quarter, up about 1,127% from the same quarter a year earlier, and that third-quarter growth of around 47% was down from 144% in the second quarter and 132% in the first. CNBC said revenue for the nine months ended 30 September was $33.24 billion, up roughly 1,200% from a year earlier. Reuters said the third-quarter net loss was $23.29 billion, down from $66.3 billion the quarter before. CNBC reported that same third-quarter net loss of $23.29 billion. Reuters said the operating loss in the third quarter was $567 million, compared with operating income of $974 million in the second quarter. Reuters said the operating loss is the cost of running the business, including computing and research, and that the net loss also includes non-operating items related to bonds that convert into shares. CNBC said the nine-month net loss was $104 billion, though most of that was the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities, and that the loss over the same stretch in 2025 was $25.1 billion. In the amendment, as CNBC quotes it, Anthropic said it has purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, “substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.” Reuters said the company expects to incur nearly half of that $895.4 billion before 31 December 2030, with about $69.8 billion due in the 12 months after 30 September 2026. Reuters said Anthropic incurred $5 billion in additional compute costs during the quarter, and that this reduced revenue per dollar of compute from the quarter before. Reuters does not say by how much. Reuters quoted the filing: certain compute providers and infrastructure partners depend on third-party financing or credit support to acquire chips and develop capacity, and if that financing becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered. Reuters said Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 of revenue on a trailing 12-month basis as of 30 September, up from more than 1,500 at the end of 2025. CNBC said compute and infrastructure expenses rose by $14.4 billion for the nine months, up 329% from a year earlier.
stories.matters: A buyer reading only the net loss will think the quarter cost $23.29 billion to run. Reuters says the operating loss was $567 million.
stories.imply: Do not put $23.29 billion, or $104 billion, on a slide as the cost of serving Claude. Say which line it is. Do not turn 47% growth into a dollar figure for the quarter before. Reuters does not print that quarter’s revenue.
uses: Write the quarter as Reuters gives it: revenue $16.96 billion, up 47% from the quarter before; net loss $23.29 billion; operating loss $567 million. If you use CNBC’s “roughly $17 billion,” say it is CNBC’s rounding of the same quarter.
Keep the $895.4 billion as a commitment. Reuters says about $69.8 billion is due in the 12 months after 30 September 2026. Do not call the rest a bill for this year.

If a vendor’s capacity depends on someone else’s financing, the filing line Reuters quotes is the one to put in the renewal note: contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered.
stories.example: A procurement lead renewing a Claude minimum updates the one-pager. The third quarter, as Reuters reports the 2 November amendment, is $16.96 billion of revenue and a $567 million operating loss. The $23.29 billion net loss stays in a second line, with CNBC’s note that the nine-month $104 billion is mostly the value of convertible notes. The $895.4 billion stays labeled as commitments, with $69.8 billion due in the next 12 months.
stories.audience: Anyone who buys Claude against a minimum, signs a capacity deal, or has to tell a board what Anthropic’s quarter was.
stories.watch: Whether a later amendment revises $16.96 billion, $23.29 billion or $567 million. Whether Anthropic or a cloud partner says a commitment slipped. Whether the “more than 11,900” customers at $100,000 is updated. The model names did not change with this filing.

source.title: Reuters, via Investing.com: Anthropic revenue growth slows ahead of IPO, 2 November 2026
source.quote: Certain of our compute providers and infrastructure partners depend on third-party financing or credit support to acquire chips and develop capacity, and if such financing or support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered.

stories.theme: Turkey opened a competition probe of Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode, and ordered interim terms
stories.changed: On Monday 2 November 2026 Turkey’s Competition Authority published an English notice, dated 2.11.2026, that an investigation has been launched under Article 41 of Act no 4054. The question is whether Alphabet Inc., Google Ireland Limited, Google LLC, Google International LLC and Google Reklamcılık ve Pazarlama Ltd. Şti. violated Article 6 through AI Overviews and AI Mode in Google Search. The notice says a preliminary inquiry, begun with a board decision dated 27 August 2026 and numbered 26-31/932-M, examined four things: whether those features changed how people get information and hurt traffic to news publishers and other content creators; whether the terms in publisher agreements are unfair; whether the features shut out publishers, other creators and AI chatbots; and whether publishers were treated differently when their content was chosen or licensed for the features. The notice says that, because the indications of exclusionary and exploitative behavior toward news publishers had reached the level of strong suspicion, the board also decided, at its meeting of 8 October 2026, decision 26-37/1000-423, to impose interim measures under Article 9.4. The measures concern Google’s use of news publishers’ content in AI Overviews and AI Mode, and the contract terms for that use. The notice says the measures are to ensure that Google sets conditions which would not lead to discrimination among news publishers, which reflect the economic value of using their content, and which let publishers set their options for that use independently of their visibility and indexing on Google’s other services. The notice does not say the board found a violation. It does not name a fine.
stories.matters: A publisher’s choice about the AI summary is supposed to be separable from whether the page stays in ordinary Search, and that is an order while the case is open, not a verdict.
stories.imply: Do not tell a newsroom the case is won, or that a fine has been set. Do tell them the interim terms are already the board’s decision of 8 October, announced on 2 November, and that one of the three terms is a choice that is not tied to indexing.
uses: Write the status as “investigation announced 2 November 2026; interim measures decided 8 October 2026.” The defendants named on the page are the Alphabet and Google companies listed above.

If a contract says a publisher must allow AI Overviews in order to stay indexed, that is the term the order describes as something publishers should be able to set separately. The page does not say Google has already changed the contract.
Keep “strong suspicion” as the board’s words for why it ordered interim measures. It is not a finding that Article 6 was broken.
stories.example: A publisher that licenses stories to Google adds one line to the contract review: Turkey’s authority, on 2 November, said publishers should be able to choose whether their content is used in AI Overviews and AI Mode without that choice deciding their indexing elsewhere. The line is an interim measure. The investigation has not ended, and no fine is on the page.
stories.audience: News publishers, search and content-licensing teams, and anyone who has to say whether an AI summary is optional or part of being in Google.
stories.watch: Whether Google changes the publisher terms, or says the existing control already meets the order. Whether the board finds a violation or names a fine. Whether the 27 August inquiry or the 8 October decision is published in full, beyond this notice.

source.title: Turkish Competition Authority: investigation and interim measures on Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, 2 November 2026
source.quote: allow publishers to set their options concerning the use of their content in the relevant services independently of their visibility and indexing on other services provided by Google.

stories.theme: The New York Times sued Brave over an index the complaint says holds more than 30 billion pages
stories.changed: On Monday 2 November 2026 TechCrunch reported that the New York Times sued Brave, alleging it scraped the Times’s copyrighted content and unlawfully distributed it to customers the suit names as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI and Cohere. TechCrunch said a separate lawsuit, filed the same day by the New York Daily News, the Chicago Tribune and the Orlando Sentinel, was brought in federal court in Manhattan as well. TechCrunch says the Times likens Brave to a supplier, dealer and distributor of stolen copyrighted content, and quotes the suit: “In this way, Brave acts both like a burglar that misappropriates the content of publishers, and an AI ‘fence’ that sells stolen content to third parties.” TechCrunch says the suit says Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages using an unidentified crawler, so publishers could not block it. TechCrunch says the suit also targets a browser feature that bypasses paywalls, and Brave’s practice of blocking publishers’ ads while selling its own. TechCrunch says the Times seeks an injunction and damages. It does not print a damages number. TechCrunch says Brave did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Verge, the same day, quotes a complaint by the Daily News, the Chicago Tribune and the Orlando Sentinel saying Brave has monetized an index by providing AI companies with paid access to “real-time online content from the Brave Index,” and that those companies use the index to train models, to answer queries, or both. The Verge quotes that complaint: “Brave has never asked for the Publishers’ permission to access their websites, much less to copy the material and provide it to users or other AI companies.” The Verge quotes Times spokesperson Graham James: “While we believe in the ethical and responsible use and development of AI, Brave has flouted established copyright law and ignored repeated requests by The Times to stop its infringing conduct.” The Verge quotes Steven Lieberman, the attorney for the other three publications: “Buying stolen goods secondhand doesn’t make them legitimate.” The Verge says Perplexity’s chief communications officer, Jesse Dwyer, said: “The New York Times is overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists. (Who could’ve easily identified the disinformation in this suit.)” The Verge says Brave, Anthropic, Mistral, SpaceXSI and Cohere did not immediately reply. A Verge update the same day says the three-paper suit was filed by those publications, not by the companies that run them.
stories.matters: A search index sold to a model can be the thing a publisher sues, even when the model company is named as a customer and is not the defendant.
stories.imply: If a product answers from “the Brave Index,” or from a feed whose crawler you cannot name in robots.txt, this complaint is the allegation to put on the review. It is not a ruling. No damages figure has been published.
uses: Name the two suits. The Times sued Brave and named Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI and Cohere as customers, TechCrunch says. The Daily News, the Chicago Tribune and the Orlando Sentinel sued separately, the same day, in Manhattan.

If the appeal of an index is that the crawler is not named, that is the fact the Times complaint treats as the problem. TechCrunch says the suit says publishers could not block an unidentified crawler.
Do not add a damages number. TechCrunch says the Times seeks an injunction and damages, and does not print an amount. Brave had not commented, TechCrunch says. Perplexity had, the Verge says.
stories.example: A team that buys a web index for a support bot writes down the 2 November suits before the renewal. The Times complaint, as TechCrunch reports it, says the index holds more than 30 billion pages and was sold on to named model companies. The note says Brave had not commented, that Perplexity called the suit disinformation, and that no court has set a sum.
stories.audience: Anyone who buys a web index for an assistant, or who has to explain where an answer’s pages came from.
stories.watch: Whether Brave answers. Whether a judge sets a schedule or a sum. Whether any named customer says it has stopped using the index. Whether the “more than 30 billion” figure is revised in an amended complaint.

source.title: TechCrunch: New York Times and other outlets sue Brave over alleged content scraping, 2 November 2026
source.quote: In this way, Brave acts both like a burglar that misappropriates the content of publishers, and an AI ‘fence’ that sells stolen content to third parties.

stories.theme: Musk said serving Grok Bot cost too much next to revenue, and did not say the new limit
stories.changed: On Sunday 1 November 2026 Elon Musk replied on X to a user, DogecoinNorway. The whole reply was: “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.” TechCrunch, on Monday 2 November, said some Grok Bot users found their weekly usage limits maxed out over Halloween weekend even if they had not been using the agent overnight. TechCrunch said some users reported on X that their usage jumped from as low as 50% to 100%. TechCrunch said Musk confirmed in that Sunday post that this was not a glitch. TechCrunch also said he has not addressed it on his main feed, and that he has not shared how subscribers’ usage limits will be affected from here. The same evening, in a separate post, Musk wrote that Grok Bot will research gifts friends and family would love and buy them. TechCrunch says Grok Bot has been described as a success for SpaceX, which said in a filing last month that AI now makes up 52% of company income, and that the renamed Super Intelligence division turned a profit of $431 million. TechCrunch says that profit would have been higher if not for $1.2 billion of one-time costs related to the acquisition of Cursor. Those filing figures are TechCrunch’s account of last month. They are not a new allowance, and they are not in Musk’s Sunday reply.
stories.matters: A weekly agent allowance can hit the ceiling over a weekend, and the only official sentence so far does not say what the ceiling is.
stories.imply: Do not plan a week of Grok Bot work against last week’s meter. Do not write a new cap, or a price, into the ticket. Musk’s reply does not contain one, and TechCrunch says he has not published the next limit.
uses: Quote the sentence and the date: 1 November 2026, a reply, not a help-page update. TechCrunch on 2 November says he has not said how limits change.
If someone says the meter moved from 50% to 100%, say that is what some users reported, as TechCrunch describes those posts. It is not a figure SpaceX has confirmed as the size of a cut.
Keep last month’s filing, as TechCrunch reports it, off the allowance. AI at 52% of income, a $431 million profit and $1.2 billion of Cursor costs do not say how many tasks a seat gets this week.
stories.example: A team that runs a Monday agent queue on Grok Bot checks the meter before it loads the week. TechCrunch says some meters were already full on Sunday, and Musk’s reply named the cost, not a new number of tasks. The lead writes that down and does not invent the cap.
stories.audience: Anyone who budgets a week of agent work on a flat Grok Bot or Cursor seat, and the people who have to explain a sudden stop.
stories.watch: Whether SpaceX or Cursor publishes the new weekly limit, or says the weekend meters were a fault and will be restored. Whether a help page gets a date. Musk’s gift post the same evening is not that page.

source.title: Elon Musk on X, replying about Grok Bot, 1 November 2026
source.quote: The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue

stories.theme: OpenAI’s Georgia campus agreement includes up to 1,000 megawatts it can stop drawing, and the campus is not running
stories.changed: On Monday 2 November 2026 OpenAI announced the Grid Protectors Program. The post says OpenAI will work with utilities, regulators and policymakers so that future campuses reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain. It says the arrangements will differ by location, and that further commitments will be shared as they are finalized. For a planned campus in Effingham County, Georgia, the post says OpenAI has committed to pay the full infrastructure and electric-service costs required to serve the project. It says that once the campus is operating, OpenAI can reduce the power it draws during times of need. It says the agreement with Georgia Power also includes up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response, “freeing up power to help keep air conditioning running in hundreds of thousands of homes during extreme heat.” The next sentence says that, for scale, this is equivalent to the average electricity demand of roughly 700,000 households, and more households than Washington, D.C., and Boston combined. The post says the campus is still in development, and that OpenAI intends Effingham to be a pilot. It says Georgia Power says this flexibility can reduce the amount of new generation the utility needs to build. It says the utility projects approximately $950 million in annual customer savings beginning in 2029 from its portfolio of large-load agreements and expected growth, including Project Camellia, and estimates a benefit of at least $15 a month for a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours. Those two figures are the utility’s projection for that portfolio, as OpenAI reports it. The post does not say they are the saving from Effingham alone. It also says flexibility cannot replace investment in new supply and transmission.
stories.matters: The number a neighbour will hear is up to 1,000 megawatts given back in a strain. The campus that would do it is still in development.
stories.imply: Do not tell a council the campus is already keeping the air conditioning on, or that customers are already saving $950 million or $15 a month because of it. The post says the campus is not operating, and it ties those savings to a wider portfolio.
uses: Write “up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response” and “campus still in development.” OpenAI’s “roughly 700,000 households” is its scale for that megawatt figure. It is not a list of homes served.

If a slide uses $950 million a year from 2029, or at least $15 a month, say OpenAI attributes those estimates to Georgia Power’s portfolio of large-load agreements and expected growth, including Project Camellia.
The post says OpenAI has committed to pay the full infrastructure and electric-service costs to serve the Effingham project. That is a commitment about a campus that is not operating yet.
stories.example: A facilities lead asked whether the Georgia campus already frees power for the county writes the answer from the 2 November post: the agreement includes up to 1,000 megawatts of demand the campus can stop drawing, once it is operating. It is not operating. The household figure is OpenAI’s comparison. The $950 million is Georgia Power’s portfolio projection, as the post reports it.
stories.audience: Anyone who sites a compute campus, talks to a utility, or has to correct a claim that an AI site is already propping up the local grid.
stories.watch: Whether Effingham gets an operating date. Whether any other campus is added to Grid Protectors with its own megawatt figure. Whether Georgia Power’s $950 million projection is revised, or is ever tied to this campus alone.

signals.raw: Anthropic amendment, 2 Nov. Reuters: third-quarter revenue $16.96 billion, up 47%; net loss $23.29 billion; operating loss $567 million, after operating income of $974 million the quarter before. CNBC: nine-month revenue $33.24 billion; nine-month net loss $104 billion, mostly convertible notes. Commitments about $895.4 billion. Reuters: about $69.8 billion due in the 12 months after 30 Sept 2026. Not a new model.

Turkish Competition Authority, notice dated 2 Nov: investigation of Google AI Overviews and AI Mode under Act 4054. Interim measures decided 8 Oct (decision 26-37/1000-423), after a preliminary inquiry dated 27 Aug. Publishers should be able to set AI use independently of indexing. Strong suspicion, not a finding, and no fine on the page.

TechCrunch, 2 Nov: the Times sued Brave and named Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI and Cohere as customers of the index. The complaint, as TechCrunch quotes it, says the index holds more than 30 billion pages. No damages figure. Brave had not commented. The Verge quotes Perplexity calling the suit disinformation.

Elon Musk, 1 Nov, on X: “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.” TechCrunch, 2 Nov: some users reported meters jumping from as low as 50% to 100%. He has not said how the limits change. Last month’s filing figures in that piece, 52% of income and a $431 million profit, are not a new allowance.

OpenAI, 2 Nov: Grid Protectors. Planned Effingham County campus is still in development. Georgia Power agreement includes up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response. OpenAI says that scale is roughly 700,000 households. Georgia Power’s $950 million a year from 2029 is a portfolio projection, as the post reports it, not Effingham alone.
